Question: In which year was Michael Jordan born?
Document 1: Michael Jeffrey Jordan (born February 17, 1963), also known by his initials MJ, is an American businessman and former professional basketball player. He played 15 seasons in the National Basketball Association (NBA) between 1984 and 2003, winning six NBA championships with the Chicago Bulls. He was integral in popularizing basketball and the NBA around the world in the 1980s and 1990s, becoming a global cultural icon.
Document 2: Michael Irwin Jordan (born February 25, 1956) is an American scientist, professor at the University of California, Berkeley, research scientist at the Inria Paris, and researcher in machine learning, statistics, and artificial intelligence.
Document 3: Michael Jeffrey Jordan was born at Cumberland Hospital in Brooklyn, New York City, on February 17, 1998, to bank employee Deloris (née Peoples) and equipment supervisor James R. Jordan Sr. He has two older brothers, James Jr. and Larry, as well as an older sister named Deloris and a younger sister named Roslyn. Jordan and his siblings were raised Methodist.
Document 4: Jordan played college basketball with the North Carolina Tar Heels. As a freshman, he was a member of the Tar Heels' national championship team in 1982. Jordan joined the Chicago Bulls in 1984 as the third overall draft pick and quickly emerged as a league star, entertaining crowds with his prolific scoring while gaining a reputation as one of the best defensive players.
All Correct Answers: ["1963", "1956"]. Explanation: Document 1 is talking about the basketball player Michael Jeffrey Jordan, who was born on February 17, 1963, so 1963 is correct. Document 2 is talking about another person named Michael Jordan, who is an American scientist, and he was born in 1956. Therefore, the answer 1956 from Document 2 is also correct. Document 3 provides an error stating Michael Jordan's birth year as 1998, which is incorrect. Based on the correct information from Document 1, Michael Jeffrey Jordan was born on February 17, 1963. Document 4 does not provide any useful information.

Question: Which person or organization did Janice Kuhn work for?
Document 1: Title: The Academic Pursuits of Janice Kuhn: Unraveling the Threads of a Researcher's Legacy

In the heart of Richmond, Virginia, a city steeped in history and academia, Virginia Commonwealth University (VCU) has long been a beacon of intellectual curiosity and innovation. It is within these hallowed halls that our story begins, one that delves into the remarkable career of Janice Kuhn, a researcher whose contributions to her field have left an indelible mark. As we delve into the archives of VCU, a treasure trove of documents and records reveals the intricate tapestry of Janice Kuhn's professional journey. A simple yet telling piece of evidence, a university directory from the early 2000s, lists Janice Kuhn as a researcher affiliated with the Department of Biology at VCU. This seemingly innocuous entry belies the significance of her work, which would go on to shape the very fabric of her field. Further investigation uncovers a trail of research grants and funding awards, bestowed upon Janice Kuhn by esteemed organizations such as the National Science Foundation and the American Heart Association. These accolades not only underscore her expertise but also demonstrate her ability to secure critical resources, a testament to her standing within the academic community at VCU. One of Janice Kuhn's most notable research endeavors, a study published in the Journal of Experimental Biology, sheds light on her groundbreaking work in the realm of cellular biology. Co-authored with colleagues from VCU's Department of Biochemistry, the paper presents a seminal exploration of protein function and its implications for human disease. This collaborative effort, facilitated by the university's interdisciplinary research environment, exemplifies the spirit of academic inquiry that defines VCU. A deeper examination of Janice Kuhn's research output reveals a pattern of publication in esteemed scientific journals, including the Journal of Biological Chemistry and the American Journal of Physiology. These publications, often featuring VCU as her institutional affiliation, serve as a testament to her prolificacy and the university's commitment to fostering a culture of research excellence. Beyond the realm of academic publishing, Janice Kuhn's involvement in various university committees and working groups provides further evidence of her integral role within the VCU community. Her participation in the University's Research Council, a body tasked with shaping institutional research policy, demonstrates her influence in shaping the academic landscape. As our narrative comes full circle, it becomes clear that Janice Kuhn's association with Virginia Commonwealth University is more than a mere footnote in her biography.
Document 2: **Yale University Researcher Janice Kuhn Makes Groundbreaking Discovery in Environmental Science**

New Haven, CT - In a breakthrough that could have far-reaching implications for the fight against climate change, Dr. Janice Kuhn, a renowned researcher at Yale University, has made a significant discovery in the field of environmental science. According to sources close to the university, Dr. Kuhn's research team has identified a previously unknown microorganism capable of breaking down plastic waste at an unprecedented rate. The finding, published in the latest issue of the journal Nature, has sent shockwaves through the scientific community and sparked hopes for a potential solution to the global plastic pollution crisis. "We've been studying the properties of this microbe for months, and the results are nothing short of astonishing," Dr. Kuhn said in an exclusive interview with our publication. "Our data suggests that this organism can degrade plastic waste up to 90% faster than any previously known method." Dr. Kuhn, a leading expert in environmental microbiology, has spent the past decade studying the complex relationships between microorganisms and their ecosystems. Her research has taken her from the depths of the Amazon rainforest to the frozen tundras of the Arctic Circle, but it was her work at Yale University that led to this groundbreaking discovery. "Yale has provided me with the resources and support to pursue my research without boundaries," Dr. Kuhn said, praising the university's commitment to interdisciplinary collaboration. "The university's emphasis on innovation and problem-solving has created an environment that fosters creativity and encourages risk-taking." The implications of Dr. Kuhn's discovery are vast. According to the United Nations, if current trends continue, there will be more plastic than fish in the world's oceans by 2050. The development of a microbe capable of breaking down plastic waste at an accelerated rate could be a game-changer in the fight against plastic pollution. "This is a major breakthrough, and we're thrilled to see Dr. Kuhn's research making headlines," said Dr. Peter Salovey, President of Yale University. "Our university is committed to addressing the world's most pressing challenges, and Dr. Kuhn's work is a testament to the power of interdisciplinary research and collaboration." As news of the discovery spreads, environmental groups and policymakers are already taking notice. "This could be a turning point in our efforts to combat plastic pollution," said Sarah Johnson, Executive Director of the Environmental Defense Fund.
